stem: After a year of rapid growth, a fintech company's IAM roles still carry the broad permissions granted during early development. The security lead wants to shrink each role to what it actually uses, based on evidence rather than guesswork. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Replace each role's custom policies with the AWS managed PowerUserAccess job function policy
Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate a policy for each role from its CloudTrail activity, then test and attach it
Turn on an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer for the account and remove every role that appears in its findings
Turn on the AWS Trusted Advisor IAM Access Key Rotation check and rotate the credentials it flags
Review IAM last accessed information and remove the services and actions that each role has not used

rationale: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation reviews CloudTrail events for a role over a date range and produces a policy template that contains only the actions the role used, which you test and then attach. IAM last accessed information shows which allowed services and actions each identity has actually used, so unused permissions can be removed. An Access Analyzer external access analyzer finds resource-based policies that share a resource with a principal outside your zone of trust; it does not review whether a role's own permissions are used, so it would not flag an overly broad role that only ever acts inside the account. The Trusted Advisor IAM Access Key Rotation check flags IAM access keys that have not been rotated in 90 days; it says nothing about which permissions a role's policy grants, so rotating keys does not shrink anything.
